results.summary: This design implements a small feedforward artificial neural network accelerator with a 4-5-1 topology, using fixed-point arithmetic for activations and weights. It is controlled via an SPI-like interface that separates weight loading from inference, allowing repeated calculations without resending weights. The chip includes four bring-up modes—normal, heartbeat, loopback, and self-test—selectable by pins, to aid post-fabrication verification without external hardware. Notable for its compact, time-multiplexed datapath and built-in self-test, it requires an SPI-capable host for real inference tasks.

This mixed-signal chip integrates an 8-bit tracking analog-to-digital converter and an on-chip process variation monitor. The ADC uses analog pins for a reference voltage and input signal, while the process monitor outputs ring oscillator frequencies to assess fabrication variations. It is designed for analog and variation-sensing applications, with digital outputs for the ADC count and oscillator signals. The design is notable for combining these functions in a single Tiny Tapeout tile, but detailed usage and test procedures are not provided.

This design implements an 8-entry, 8-bit content-addressable memory (CAM) that supports exact matching, masked pattern matching, and priority-based resolution. It can be configured via control pins to write data, load masks, and search, returning the address of the highest-priority match within one clock cycle. The CAM is intended for compact pattern-matching and lookup tasks, such as network routing or data filtering. The project includes thorough documentation and is verified with Cocotb and gate-level tests.

This design is an 8-bit, 16-word dual-port RAM with arbitration and write-collision detection, fitting in a single Tiny Tapeout tile. It uses a shared multiplexed address/data bus and control signals to select ports and perform reads or writes, with outputs indicating collision and grant status. The RAM can be accessed independently from two ports, and simultaneous writes to the same address are detected. Verified with Cocotb tests, it requires no external hardware for operation on the demo board.

This project implements a 4-bit Vedic multiplier, which multiplies two 4-bit numbers using a Vedic mathematics algorithm. The design is purely combinational, with inputs and outputs directly mapped to the chip pins. There is no documentation beyond the title and pin names, so the exact implementation details and testing procedures are unclear. It appears to be a simple educational or demonstration design.

This design displays a cellular automaton on a VGA screen, outputting RGB and sync signals compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. The project title indicates the core function, but no details on the automaton rules, operation, or testing are provided. It requires a VGA monitor and the Tiny VGA PMOD for output. The documentation is essentially empty, leaving the implementation and usage unclear.

VITAL-AP is an adaptive 8-bit pixel register designed for low-power image and video processing, deciding whether to update or hold its value based on pixel value, transition magnitude, temporal behavior, edge activity, and motion activity. It aims to reduce switching activity and dynamic power by suppressing unnecessary updates, with controls for sensitivity, prediction enable, force update, and various awareness modes. The design can be tested with provided Verilog and Cocotb testbenches covering static, small, and large transitions, sequences, and force-update. It is a research-oriented project, but no silicon results are reported.

This analog design implements an integrate-and-fire neuron based on the van Schaik 2001 model, with a buffered membrane voltage output and multiple inputs. It is an analog circuit intended for neuromorphic computing applications. The project documentation is minimal, providing only the title, one-line description, and pin names, with no details on operation or testing. External hardware and usage instructions are not specified.

This analog IP integrates a Banba current-mode bandgap reference (1.2V) and a folded-cascode low-dropout regulator (1.8V output) in Sky130. It includes digital trim inputs for calibration and enable signals for a sink and ring oscillator, with analog outputs for the reference and regulated voltage. The design is intended for on-chip voltage regulation and reference generation in mixed-signal systems. Documentation is sparse, providing only a basic overview without detailed testing or usage instructions.

This Wokwi-based project converts an 8-bit binary input into signals for a 7-segment display to show hexadecimal digits. It takes eight input bits and drives seven segment outputs plus presumably a decimal point. The documentation is essentially empty beyond the title, so implementation details and testing are not described. It requires a 7-segment display for output, and is a simple educational design.
